claims.text: A random spatial distribution of elements with differing atomic sizes induces local lattice distortion in high-entropy alloys.
Local lattice distortion acts as a barrier to dislocation motion.
Lattice-distortion-mediated inhibition of dislocations governs the enhanced hardness and strength of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed test material is a single-phase equiatomic BCC or FCC high-entropy alloy with substantial atomic-size mismatch.
Changing composition can be used to reduce or enhance atomic-size mismatch while retaining similar phase and grain structures.
Applying identical thermal and mechanical treatments while controlling phase and grain structure is intended to isolate the effect of lattice distortion on mechanical behavior.
Local lattice distortion is manifested as variation in interatomic distances.
Greater atomic-radius mismatch produces greater local strain and lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion raises the energy barrier for dislocation glide.
A higher barrier to dislocation glide increases yield strength and hardness.
Alloys with greater atomic-size mismatch and lattice distortion will have higher hardness and yield strength than a lower-mismatch baseline with comparable phase and grain structure.
The higher-mismatch alloys will exhibit greater hindrance of dislocation motion in microstructural observations.
The baseline is a high-entropy alloy with comparable phase and grain structure but elements of more similar atomic radii and therefore reduced lattice distortion.
The proposed relationship should hold primarily for single-phase solid solutions when grain size, processing history, and secondary precipitation are controlled.
The relationship may fail when multiphase structures, precipitate hardening, or other extrinsic strengthening mechanisms dominate the mechanical response.
The quantitative contribution of lattice-strain dislocation pinning relative to precipitation or intermetallic strengthening remains unresolved.
X-ray diffraction can be used in the comparison to confirm phase consistency and assess lattice strain.
TEM can be used to compare dislocation behavior and interactions with distorted lattice regions.

Failure of the higher-mismatch alloy to show a statistically significant increase in both hardness and yield strength, or failure to show additional dislocation hindrance by TEM, is designated as falsifying evidence.
